intro: How each roof's estimate is made, from the data sources to the money. Pick a step, then a part of it: what it does, why, what else could work, where it goes wrong and how to change it.

steps.title: Build the 3D landscape
steps.summary: Building outlines, a laser scan of every roof and tree, and aerial photos, all from LINZ.

items.title: Which buildings exist
items.text: Every building outline in an area comes from LINZ's NZ Building Outlines, picked by the suburb, town and council LINZ records on each outline.
items.why: LINZ's outlines are the one open, national list of buildings, and each keeps its ID from one build to the next, so a roof's fixes and reports stay attached to it.
try: Outlines traced from the laser scan, for houses LINZ has not drawn yet
Outlines read from the newest aerial photo by an image model

known: A house built since LINZ last drew the area has no outline, so no estimate.

items.title: A laser scan of the roofs
items.text: LINZ's LiDAR survey for the area: the raw point cloud (from OpenTopography's copy) where it has been published, and LINZ's surface model otherwise. Only points classed as building are used for roofs. The ground model and surface model give trees, neighbours and hills.
items.why: A laser scan measures height to a few centimetres, so a roof's slope and direction are measured, not guessed from a photo. The raw points keep detail the gridded surface smooths away.
try: Heights from overlapping aerial photos where the scan is old
Using two surveys of different years together

known: A roof built or changed since the survey is read as it was then.
Where the raw points are not published, small roof detail is lost in the surface model.

items.title: Distant hills
items.text: LINZ's national elevation model, out past the area, for hills on the horizon.
items.why: The laser scan stops at the survey's edge, but mountains far beyond it block the low sun. The national model covers every hill at a size a build can read quickly.
try: A finer elevation model where one covers the hills
Checking horizons against photos taken from real roofs

known: LINZ calls this model cartographic, not precise: a ridge can be metres off.

items.title: Aerial photos
items.text: LINZ aerial photos, the newest that cover the area, for roof lines and objects on roofs. The map itself shows LINZ Basemaps' photo.
items.why: The photo shows roof lines, skylights and vents that the scan blurs, and it is usually newer than the scan.
try: Sharper photos where a council has them
Older photos, to see roofs before trees grew over them

known: Without a photo, a build skips finding objects from the photo.

items.title: Places with no laser scan
items.text: Where no LiDAR survey exists, roofs are modelled from the outline: a gable or hipped roof at 20° for houses and flat for large buildings. Every such building says so on the map.
items.why: A plain, modest roof gives a fair first estimate where there is nothing to measure, and the map says it is a guess rather than hiding the town.
try: Reading gable or hip from the photo's roof lines
Reading the pitch from shadows in the photo

known: Every roof in such a town gets the same pitch, so steep and shallow roofs are both off.

items.title: Lining the data up
items.text: The photo and the scan were taken in different years and lean differently. Each roof's lean is measured by matching the photos (up to 4 m), and an outline that sits off the scanned roof is slid onto it (up to 2 m) without changing its shape. A roof whose faces come from the scan's planes is laid over the map's photo directly: its lines are moved in proportion to their height until they sit on the edges the photo shows.
items.why: People judge a roof by the photo under it. Panels drawn a metre off the roof look wrong even when the sums are right, so the drawing follows the photo and the sums follow the scan.
try: Fitting the outline's shape to the scan's roof edges, not only sliding it
Correcting each photo's lean from where its camera was

steps.title: Read each roof
steps.summary: Find the roof's faces, their slope and direction, and anything on them.

items.title: Four readings of the roof
items.text: Each roof is read four ways: an image model that outlines shapes in the photo, a model trained on hand-drawn roof lines, the laser scan's flat regions, and the simplest roof form that fits. Each reading is scored on how well its edges match the lines in the photo and how well its faces fit the scan, and the best is kept.
items.why: Each reading fails on different roofs. Scoring several against the scan and the photo and keeping the best is more reliable than tuning any one of them.
try: A model trained on the hand markup that draws the roof lines directly
Letting the readings vote line by line instead of picking one whole roof

cases.defect: truncated pyramid: 4 slopes plus a real 4 m flat square at the peak

not close to the obvious faces visible in the imagery

items.title: When the reading is doubtful
items.text: A reading scoring under 0.30 is not used. One under 0.60 competes with faces found from the laser scan alone, and the scan's version wins when it explains the roof better or more simply.
items.why: A low score means the reading and the scan disagree. Faces from the scan alone are plainer, but rarely wrong in kind.
try: Learning the two limits from the hand markup instead of setting them by hand

cases.defect: invented kite-shaped face in the middle of a plain roof
unnecessary inaccurate roof lines drawn where none exist
simple roof read wrongly

outcomes: competes with faces from the scan

items.title: Roof faces from the laser scan's own planes
items.text: Flat planes are grown on the laser points themselves, and each roof line is put where two of those planes meet or where the height steps. A roof read this way is used ahead of the image models' reading; a paid reading of the photo and a hand-drawn roof still come first.
items.why: A line where two measured planes meet follows the real ridge. An edge in the photo may be a shadow, a gutter or a change of paint.
try: Stricter merging of planes on low-pitch roofs
Fitting neighbouring planes together so they share their ridge exactly

items.title: Hand-drawn roofs come first
items.text: Where a person has drawn a roof's faces and lines, the drawing is used as it is. Identical roofs in a row of houses share the reading that explains the whole set best.
items.why: A person looking at the photo is right more often than any model, and identical houses should get identical answers.
try: More people drawing roofs: every drawing fixes a roof and becomes a test
Training the reading models on each new drawing

items.title: Slope and direction
items.text: Each face gets a flat plane fitted to its laser points, ignoring points more than 30 cm off it. Faces steeper than 55° are walls, not roof. A roof whose points fit its planes less than 45% of the time gets no panels.
items.why: A fit that ignores stray points is not tilted by chimneys, gutters or overhanging trees, as a plain average would be.
try: Telling a balcony or deck from roof by its height below the eaves
Fitting all of a roof's faces at once

show.ask: A roof whose points fit its planes

items.title: Objects on the roof
items.text: Vents, skylights, chimneys and plant are found two ways: laser points standing more than 0.4 m off the roof's plane, and patches of the photo that stand out from the roof around them (within 1.2 m). Panels keep clear of both.
items.why: The scan finds things that stand up; the photo finds flat things such as skylights. Each alone misses one kind.
try: An image model trained on the drawn obstructions
The scan's return strength, to spot glass

steps.title: Sunlight
steps.summary: How much sun reaches a roof of each slope and direction over a year.

items.title: Clear-sky sun, hour by hour
items.text: The sun's path and clear-sky light for every hour of a year, from the pvlib library's Ineichen model.
items.why: Ineichen is a standard, well-tested clear-sky model, and pvlib is the open library solar engineers use, so anyone can check it.
try: Hourly sunlight from satellite records instead of a clear sky cut by cloud

items.title: Cloud, from measured records
items.text: Clear-sky sun is cut each month to what ground instruments have measured (pyranometers, which record all the sunlight reaching the ground). Near Queenstown (within about 44 km) that is NIWA's SolarView record for Queenstown, built on decades of measurements at Queenstown Airport. Elsewhere it is the nearest of 28 NIWA radiation stations, up to about 166 km away. Each roof's workings name its station and how far away it is.
items.why: Ground instruments are the most accurate measure of sunlight there is. Models are checked against them, not the other way round.
try: Satellite cloud records, which are finer in space than stations

known: A station far from a town may have a different climate from it.

items.title: Differences between towns
items.text: A station measures one spot. How much sunnier or duller each town is than its station comes from ERA5, a global weather reanalysis (a weather model corrected by satellite and weather observations), in cells about 28 km north to south by 20 km east to west, averaged over 1991–2020. Only its differences between places are used, held between 0.85 and 1.15 of the station's figure; cells averaging over 800 m high are mountains, not towns, and are left out.
items.why: A weather model gets the difference between nearby places better than the amount itself, so only its ratio is used and the measured level is kept.
try: A finer reanalysis or a satellite sunlight product

items.title: What the sunlight data cannot see
items.text: Cloud is a long-term monthly average for a place, the same every day of that month: a typical year, not this year. It is no finer than the station and the ERA5 cell, so it cannot see fog or inversion cloud that sits in one valley or town, such as winter morning fog at Wanaka or Cromwell. Where a town gets more of that than its station, its winter sun is overstated. Hills, trees and buildings are different: they are measured for every roof, from 8 m terrain and the laser scan (Shade, below).
items.why: Payback depends on a typical year. A particular year's weather would add noise, not accuracy.
try: Satellite fog records for valley towns
Measuring winter sun on a few roofs in towns that get fog

known: Valley fog is not seen, so winter sun in foggy towns is overstated.

items.title: Onto a sloped roof
items.text: Sunlight is split into direct and diffuse light (the Erbs method) and turned onto each roof slope and direction with the Perez sky model, in 5° slope by 10° direction steps.
items.why: Erbs and Perez are the standard pair in solar design tools. Working each slope and direction out once, as a table, makes every roof fast.
try: Finer slope and direction steps
A measured split of direct and diffuse light

steps.title: Shade
steps.summary: Hills, trees and buildings that block the sun, worked out for every panel.

items.title: Nearby trees and buildings
items.text: From each panel, the laser scan's surface is searched in every direction (every 4°, out to 100 m) for anything that blocks the sun.
items.why: The scan already holds every tree and neighbour, so shade is measured for each panel instead of guessed for the roof.
try: Trees that lose their leaves, letting winter sun through
Tracing the sun through the scan's points rather than its surface

known: A tree is solid all year: a bare winter tree shades as much as a summer one.

items.title: Hills
items.text: Each building's horizon of hills, in 72 directions out to 20 km, seen from its eaves, and the area's own horizon out to 30 km.
items.why: In a mountain valley the hills take the morning or evening sun. One horizon per building, from its eaves, catches that without working it out for every panel.
try: A horizon from each panel instead of each building

items.title: Deep shade
items.text: Direct sun that is blocked is taken off; light from the open sky is reduced by how much sky the panel sees. A panel keeping less than 45% of its direct sun is not placed.
items.why: A panel that sees little direct sun pays back too slowly to be worth placing.
try: Setting the limit by money (what the panel saves) instead of sunlight

steps.title: Panels and power
steps.summary: Lay panels sunniest first and work out what each one makes.

items.title: Laying out panels
items.text: 500 W panels (1.134 × 1.961 m) are packed in rows on each face, 0.10 m from edges and ridges on a small face; a face that fits more than 6 keeps 0.40 m from the roof edge and 0.30 m from ridges, unless that keeps under 75% of its panels. Portrait unless landscape fits 40% more. A face pointing away from the sun with less than 78% of the sunniest face's sun is left bare. Stray panels go: an array needs at least 3.
items.why: Fixed gaps and clean rows put panels where an installer would. Landscape is used only when it clearly fits more, because mixed rows cost more to rack.
try: Packing whole arrays at once instead of row by row
Rules taken from installers' real layouts

items.title: Sunniest first
items.text: Panels are ranked by how much they make, so a smaller system takes the best spots. The density slider fills in that order.
items.why: Most homes want fewer panels than fit. Ranking lets every system size take its own best spots.
try: Ranking by money (use at home against export) instead of energy

items.title: Power from each panel
items.text: Each panel's sunlight after shade, times its rating, less 16.4% for the inverter, heat, dirt, wiring and glass reflection. The building's total is the sum of its panels.
items.why: Each panel is worked out from its own sunlight, so a part-shaded roof is not averaged away.
try: A panel temperature model from local air temperature and wind

known: One loss figure for every system: hot, dusty or old systems lose more.

items.title: Buildings that are gone
items.text: An outline whose building no longer shows in the newest photo is withheld.
items.why: A cheap pixel check screens every outline, so the paid second look is needed only for the few it flags.
try: A free local model for the second look

cases.defect: 18 Beetham St: phantom building, knocked down -- the imagery shows it is no longer there.

items.title: Heat map mode
items.text: The heat map colours every 0.4 m of roof by its yearly sunlight, from the same sun and shade model.
items.why: The same model as the panels, so the colours and the figures never disagree.
try: Hours of direct sun in winter, as a second colour scale

steps.title: Money
steps.summary: Bills before and after, the cost, and the saving once a loan is repaid.

items.title: A household's day
items.text: Each building's use of power hour by hour, for an average day in each season: a home from the Electricity Authority's figures for its area, scaled for people and house size; a business by its floor area and its type: offices and shops from New Zealand's commercial building survey, sheds and workshops at about a third of that. Solar powers the building first; the rest is exported.
items.why: Average days by season are public and local. Real meter data for each home is neither.
try: Real smart-meter profiles, shared with consent
Profiles for homes with a heat pump or an electric car

known: Use does not follow the weather, so a cold, dull week costs the same as an average one.

items.title: Batteries
items.text: A battery charges only from spare solar. On a time-of-use plan it saves its charge for peak hours, giving off-peak only what the coming peak will not need before the sun refills it; on a flat plan it covers any shortfall as it comes. Each season's typical day is repeated until the battery's charge settles, and the charts show it charging and powering the home.
items.why: Charging only from spare solar is how most home batteries are set up, and it keeps the saving from solar apart from tariff tricks.
try: Charging from the grid off-peak on a time-of-use plan

known: A typical day repeated cannot show a run of dull days.

items.title: The whole year, day by day
items.text: The year chart has a different day for every day of the year. Each hour's use and solar follow a smooth curve through the year that keeps each season's average day exactly, and each day's sunlight follows a real year's weather at the roof (the last full year of the ERA-five record), rescaled so each season makes what the bills say. The battery carries its charge from one day to the next. Use does not follow the weather. The bills are still worked out on the four average days; the chart shows how far the day-by-day year's grid use differs from them.
items.why: A real year's weather shows the swings an average day hides, while the bills stay on the averages they were checked against.
try: Working the bills out on the day-by-day year too

known: One year's weather: a duller or sunnier year would differ.

items.title: Power prices
items.text: Home prices are the Electricity Authority's latest for Queenstown (Aurora Energy) (2026-05): 33.55c a kWh and $2.02 a day for a standard-use home, incl. GST. The one price is split into 49c in peak hours and 25c off-peak, so a typical home pays about the same average. Areas on another network use its prices: Central Otago (Aurora Energy) 40.69c and $1.99 a day; Southland (The Power Company) 31.28c and $3.38 a day. Businesses pay energy prices, 22c peak and 12c off-peak; their network and connection charges are a separate bill that solar does not change. Exported solar earns 12c a kWh in the day and 23c at peak in the first year (retailer buy-back rates). The prices are refreshed each month.
items.why: The Electricity Authority publishes the same figures for every network each month, so every area is priced the same way and the prices update themselves.
try: Real retail plans, retailer by retailer

known: Splitting one price into peak and off-peak only approximates real plans.

items.title: Cost and savings
items.text: The cost per kW falls with system size (Assumptions & pricing). Over a 30-year life power prices rise 4.0% a year, export rates fall 2.0% a year and panels lose 0.5% a year, shown in today's dollars.
items.why: Today's dollars make a saving late in the system's life comparable with one now.
try: Installer quotes by region in place of one cost curve

known: One cost curve for every roof: a hard roof to work on costs more.

items.title: Net saving with a loan
items.text: The green box: an average year over the loan, in today's dollars. Bill savings, less the repayments on a loan for the system (and battery) at 5.5% over 30 years. Replacements are added to the loan when they fall due and repaid with interest by its end: the inverter in year 16, and a battery in year 15 at 70% of today's price. Paid upfront, they are paid in cash in their year. The repayment is fixed, so 2.0% inflation makes it smaller in today's dollars each year.
items.why: Most households would borrow. What is left each year after repayments is the figure they can act on.
try: Green home-loan top-ups at mortgage rates

items.title: Return on investment
items.text: Paid upfront: the yearly rate the cost earns over the system's life, after inflation, replacements included. With a loan nothing is paid up front, so the return is the net saving a year.
items.why: A rate of return compares solar with other uses of the same money.
try: Years to pay back, shown beside the rate

known: The rate assumes the price rises above hold for the whole life.

steps.title: Checks and publishing
steps.summary: Every figure is re-worked and checked before it reaches the map.

items.title: Every figure shows its workings
items.text: Tap a number on a building's card to see the sum that made it. The map re-works every panel's power from the published inputs and refuses to publish on any mismatch.
items.why: A figure anyone can open and add up again is one they can trust, or show to be wrong.
try: A public page of what changed in each release, roof by roof

markup.title: Scored blind against the hand-drawn roofs
steps: Switch the change on and off with its switch, so both runs see the same roofs.
Build the development roofs as if nobody had drawn them, and score what comes out against the drawings: face overlap, roof lines found, objects found.
Fix rules against the development set only. Score the held-back set once, at the end.
Where no one has drawn a roof, the owner judges before and after side by side, shuffled, without labels.

layout.title: The same roofs, change off and on
steps: Run the build's own layout code on a sample of roofs with the change off, then on.
Count what a sound layout never does: panels off the building, across a ridge, on an object.
After a build, no roof should lose roof-face area. Render every roof that moved.

energy.title: Worked examples, and the browser against Python
steps: The worked examples can be checked by hand: a panel's kWh, an hour of sun.
The browser must give the same kWh as the build for real panels.
A change to the sun model or panel figures regenerates that fixture and needs a full rebuild.
Compare with an independent model such as PVGIS on a few roofs.

money.title: Worked examples and checks on the page
steps: The tests price fixed homes and compare with sums worked by hand.
On the page, every roof's money pill must equal its card's figure.

inputs.title: Same buildings, same areas
steps: The fetch tests check which buildings and layers an area gets.
A new source must give the same buildings where the old one covers them.
The deploy gate compares the whole build with the live map before it is published.

release.title: The deploy gate
steps: Every release is compared with the live map: roofs that lose panels, figures that disagree.
Each flagged roof is rendered and judged before the release goes out.
